findings.title: Cleanup ticker reduced below the cleanup timeout, allows overlapping runs
findings.body: The ticker interval was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1, but srv.clean has a 9-minute timeout (const timeout = 9 * time.Minute). The original 10-minute interval was deliberately chosen to be longer than the timeout so that the next tick cannot fire while a cleanup is still in flight; with a 1-minute interval, if any single cleanup takes more than one minute - which is quite plausible now that each batch does a separate SELECT and DELETE rather than a single DELETE - the next call to srv.clean will be dispatched concurrently with the previous one. There is no mutex or re-entrancy guard around srv.clean in Run, so the only thing preventing overlap was the ticker interval itself. Two concurrent cleanups performing SELECT-then-DELETE on the same annotation tables can re-introduce the very lock-contention pattern this PR is trying to eliminate, and at minimum roughly doubles steady-state database load. Either keep the interval >= the cleanup timeout, lower the timeout below 1 minute, or add a guard (sync.Mutex / atomic flag) so srv.clean cannot overlap with itself.

findings.title: r.log.Error used for routine informational log lines with nil error
findings.body: In CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) every batch is logged via r.log.Error with fields such as 'count', 'ids', 'cond' and 'affected', and each line also includes an 'err' field whose value is always nil at that point (any real error has already been returned via the if err != nil blocks). Using Error level for routine progress reports - and for explicitly nil errors - means every successful cleanup batch will be surfaced as an error to any error-rate alerting (e.g. Loki / Grafana alerting, Sentry), producing noise and potentially paging on-call. These should be Debug (or Info) level. Lines to change: 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579.

findings.title: O(n^2) string building for SQLite IN-list fallback
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a configured batch size > 999, the IN-list is built by fmt.Sprint(ids[0]) followed by a loop of fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) for each subsequent id. Each Sprintf allocates and copies the entire growing string, making the total work O(n^2) in len(ids). The new integration test exercises exactly this path with batch size 32767 and ~32k ids, so the construction cost dominates the batch. Use strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt for an O(n) build.

findings.title: SQLite IN-list branch keyed on configured batch size, not actual id count
findings.body: deleteByIDs chooses the string-interpolated IN-list based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit rather than on len(ids). When an operator configures a batch size larger than 999 but a particular fetchIDs call returns fewer matching rows than that (e.g. near the end of cleanup, or whenever fewer annotations match the WHERE clause than the batch size), the code still falls into the O(n^2) string-interpolated path even though parameterized placeholders would be safe and faster. The branch should be conditioned on len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit so the interpolation fallback is only taken when we actually have more ids than SQLite's parameter limit.
